subject: Covariance between two endogenous variables in path analyses

messages.author: f1dcc23e7cf45b5a
messages.subject: Covariance between two endogenous variables in path analyses
parts:
Dear list members,

When running a model in lavaan of the following nature: 'y1 ~ x1' and checking the modification indices, lavaan is offering to add the following connection: 'y1 ~~ x1'.  Does it make sense for both connections to exist in the same model? so 
'regressions: y1 ~ x1,
covariance: y1 ~~ x1'

Many thanks in advance!!!!

:)

messages.author: 56a8aa4a45a311ff
messages.subject: Re: Covariance between two endogenous variables in path analyses
parts:
No, it does not. You should only do modifications to the model based on MI only if there's support (theoretical or empírical). Establising both a causal and correlation between two variables is non-sense.
Warm regards,

João Marôco

messages.subject: Re: Covariance between two endogenous variables in path analyses
parts:
I think the second argument implies a covariance relationship between the error terms of Y1 and X1. So including both arguments can be acceptable if you have a theoretical basis (e.g., X1 causes Y1 and their error terms have common causes). 

Yen.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Covariance between two endogenous variables in path analyses
parts: Many circumstances could lead to this residual covariance between predictor and outcome variables. Just including the free residual covariance may only be hiding the real problem. For instance unreliability ("measurement error") in teh predictor may lead to this, in which case it would be better to address the unreliability problem than to "paper over" the problem with a residual covariance. Or it may be that an omitted predictor, correlated with the predictor in question, may be responsible. Or a selection problem might have crept into the research design. As Carl said, the causal inference literature would say that this is classic endogeneity, and their solution would be to (1) include a latent variable which jointly causes both the predictor and the outcome variable, and then (2) as Yen says, find an instrumental variable (or some more sophisticated technique) that will allow you to estimate this augmented model. One caution, however: the causal inference literature deals primary in nonparameteric estimation, while your typical SEM is linear in the parameters, so there is not a strict one-to-one betweed the two literatures (causal inference and structural equation modeling).
